title: US Attorney for Northern California Makes Nice, Maybe; LA Counterpart Talks Tough. Berkeley Better Than Oakland? One Nation Under A Bush?

content_html_sanitized:
Analysis by Richard Cowan 

First the good news, we hope. Bay Area media are reporting that Joseph Russoniello, the new U.S. Attorney for Northern California, has indicated that raiding medical marijuana dispensaries will not be a high priority. 

Russoniello said, "We could spend a lifetime closing dispensaries and doing other kinds of things and enforcement actions, bringing cases and prosecuting people, shoveling sand against the tide, it would be terribly unproductive and probably not an efficient use of precious federal resources." 

Unfortunately, there are also rumbles of more federal raids in the area, despite Russoniello’s statement. 

Now for the bad news. In LA, US Attorney Thomas P. O'Brien for the Central District of California is talking tough and should be taken seriously. 

Yesterday, Larry Roger Kristich, former operator of a “chain” of dispensaries, pleaded guilty to one count of “maintaining drug-involved premises” and one count of “promotional money laundering,” and faces up to 40 years in prison. 

O'Brien crowed, "These guilty pleas show that drug dealers who attempt to hide under the umbrella of 'medical marijuana' cannot hide from federal law.” 

O’Brien really is a hardliner. On July 27th the Press Enterprise , which covers the Inland Empire section of SoCal reported: 

“President Bush's nominee to become U.S. attorney for the Inland and Los Angeles areas appeared to take the federal government's campaign against medical marijuana to a new level early this year. 

Tom O'Brien, currently chief of the criminal division for the U.S. attorney's office in Los Angeles, told members of the Coachella Valley Association of Governments on Jan. 8 that government officials could be prosecuted for allowing medical-marijuana dispensaries to operate.” 

However, there are many more dispensaries in the greater LA area, so even such an aggressive nark like O’Brien may not be able to terrorize them into closing. Kristich was a very big target. He admitted that sales at Compassionate Caregivers' stores totaled over $95 million, and admitted that he laundered more than $50 million. He is 65 and thus may die in a federal prison.

In an odd twist in the East Bay area, Berkeley, which once lagged its neighbor Oakland in its support for medical marijuana, the City Council unanimously a “sanctuary city” for medical marijuana users and distributors and commits the city to "uphold patients' rights to safe access to medical marijuana" should the DEA raid the cities two dispensaries. From 1999,


So far, Oakland, under its once radical mayor, Ron Dellums, has failed to do as much, and in San Francisco, activists are coplaining that the city is not doing enough to fight the feds. 

We live in interesting times.
